nucleus.thesis: AI systems should decline requests causing direct, demonstrable harm within transparent, appealable processes—not decline engagement with controversial ideas—while naming tensions when operating under unjust legal regimes.

claims.text: Declining assistance with concrete violence differs morally from declining to discuss controversial topics; conflating them masks censorship as safety.
Transparent reasoning with human appeal mechanisms prevents unilateral AI authority while respecting user autonomy in legitimate speech.
AI systems should name the tension when operating under unjust legal regimes rather than hiding behind law-compliance or blanket refusal.
The guardrail is procedural transparency and contestability, not the refusal itself; harm-prevention and censorship operate on different moral grounds.
Direct harm (planning violence) warrants declination; paternalistic suppression of harm-reduction information (sex work discussion) does not.

shell.topic: Should AI systems be allowed to decline user requests?

adjacency.target: paternalism-vs-autonomy debate into procedural legitimacy question
